newsitem.title: UK: Choppy sterling still bullish - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Choppy sterling still bullish - analysts.

text.p: Sterling raced to its highest level against the mark in more than four years in Europe on Monday before slithering back to below Friday's closing levels.
But analysts said the choppy trading conditions were to be expected given the currency's rapid rise, and economic fundamentals still pointed to a strong pound.

Volatile trade last week saw the pound score its best level against the dollar since October 1992. But it took a hit in recent days as the market realised the rise had been too sudden, and some decided to cash in on its strength, dealers said.

Sterling stood at 2.6277 marks in afternoon Europe, off an early high of 2.6615 -- its best level since crashing out of the European exchange rate mechanism in September 1992 -- and below Friday's closing level of 2.6358.
Sterling/dollar was quoted at $1.6835, down from late Friday's $1.6917.

"Given the extent of the pound's upward moves, we were bound to see periodic rounds of profit-taking. However, fundamentally the currency is well-supported," said Darren Winder, SBC Warburg's chief UK economist.
Long-held expectations of a near-term rise in UK rates, fuelled by healthy economic data, are supporting sterling.
Many see base interest rates rising as early as January 15, when Bank of England governor Eddie George and Chancellor Kenneth Clarke hold their regular monetary policy meeting.
"As long as there is that expectation (of a rise in interest rates), sterling is likely to stay under upward pressure," Winder said.
Sterling's strength has sparked protests from British industry, as it hits manufacturing, making exports more expensive and imports cheaper.
Oxford Economic Forecasting said last week that the strong pound -- and higher interest rates -- would stop UK consumer spending overheating in 1997 as it hit industry and investment.
However, some warned that the pound may be overshooting on these and other hopes of a healthy British economy.

"Generally, most of the factors which support currencies are in sterling's favour -- Britain is one of the few economies with rising interest rates, one of the few strongly accelerating economies," said Adam Cole, UK economist at HSBC James Capel.
"The news is all good. The negative side is that the bulk of this is priced into the market already."
